subject: Agriculture
title: Crop Rotation Basics
description: A short lesson to help you apply Crop Rotation Basics.

hook.text: Ancient Roman farmers knew: grow wheat in the same field every year and yields collapse. Rotation was the fix.

buildup.text: Different crops draw different nutrients and host different pests. Alternating breaks disease and pest cycles.

discovery.text: A corn-soybean rotation works because soybeans add nitrogen that corn uses the following season.

twist.text: Modern monoculture replaces rotation with chemicals—synthetic nitrogen and pesticides do the work nature used to.

climax.text: Farms returning to diverse rotations often reduce input costs by 30% while maintaining yields.

punchline.text: The oldest trick in farming still works. Most farmers stopped using it.

quiz.question: Why does a corn-soybean rotation work well?
options: Soybeans fix nitrogen that corn uses the following season
Both crops repel each other's pests

details.summary: Crop rotation is the practice of growing different crops in sequence on the same field across seasons. This topic covers rotation principles, common sequences, and how alternating crops naturally manages soil fertility, pests, and diseases.
details.whyItMatters: Monoculture depletes soil and breeds resistant pests. Rotation breaks these cycles naturally, reducing the need for fertilizers and pesticides while sustaining long-term productivity.
takeaways: Alternating cereals with legumes replenishes soil nitrogen naturally
Rotation breaks pest and disease cycles that build up under monoculture
Well-planned rotations can improve yields by 10–25% compared to continuous cropping

faq.question: What is crop rotation and why do farmers practice it?
faq.answer: Crop rotation alternates different crop types on the same field each season. Each crop has different nutrient needs, root depths, and pest vulnerabilities, so rotating prevents soil depletion, disrupts pest life cycles, and maintains yields.

faq.question: What is a common crop rotation sequence?
faq.answer: A classic four-year rotation might be corn, soybeans, wheat, then a cover crop or pasture. The legume (soybeans) fixes nitrogen, the grass crops use it, and the cover crop rebuilds organic matter and suppresses weeds.
